introduction-why-sres-study-firefighting.core: The Incident Command System came from 1970s wildfires, where several agencies couldn't coordinate. Its standard roles, common terminology and scalable structure fit large software incidents that involve many teams.

first_principles.problem: Multi-team outages collapse into confusion: different terms, unclear authority, duplicated work.
derivation: Use **standard roles** (Command, Ops, Planning, Logistics, Finance/Admin).
Use **unified command** for shared ownership; respect **span of control**.

analogy.title: Three fire departments at one blaze
analogy.story: Without a shared system, one calls for water while another cuts the power. ICS gives them one plan.
analogy.breaks: Full FEMA ICS is heavy, so tech teams use a lightweight adaptation.

example.title: A multi-team outage
flow: Network, DB and app teams all respond

check.q: Why do SRE teams borrow from the FEMA Incident Command System?
check.a: It's a proven framework for coordinating many responders with standard roles, terminology and scalable structure.

the-ics-hierarchy-command-vs-general-sta.core: ICS has command staff (Incident Commander plus Public Information, Safety and Liaison officers) and general staff sections: Operations (does the work), Planning (situation, documentation, next steps), Logistics (resources) and Finance/Admin (costs, procurement).

first_principles.problem: Without functional areas, critical needs like tracking resources or documenting plans fall through the cracks.
truths: Large responses have distinct functional needs.
Structure can be assembled quickly from templates.

analogy.title: An org chart assembled in minutes
analogy.story: A temporary company, with departments, forms at the start of the emergency and dissolves after.
analogy.breaks: Most software incidents only need a subset of the sections.

example.title: A large outage's structure
flow: Logistics: get vendor support, laptops, access

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No functional gap is left unowned.

example.outcome: a complete structure for large responses.

check.q: What does the Planning section do in ICS?
check.a: It tracks the situation, maintains documentation and develops the next action plan.

mapping-fema-roles-to-software-engineeri.core: FEMA roles map directly onto tech: IC → Incident Commander; PIO → Communications Lead; Liaison → stakeholder/customer liaison; Operations → Ops Lead + SMEs; Planning → Scribe/Planning Lead; Logistics → access, tooling, vendor engagement; Finance → cost and SLA-credit tracking.

first_principles.problem: Teams find FEMA terms foreign and can't see how they apply to an outage.
derivation: **Logistics** → access, war room, vendors; **Finance** → costs, credits.

analogy.title: Translating a recipe from metric to imperial
analogy.story: Same dish, units the local cook understands.
analogy.breaks: Small companies combine many roles into one person.

example.title: Logistics in a tech incident
flow: Escalate to cloud provider premium support

check.q: What's the tech equivalent of ICS Logistics?
check.a: Securing resources: access, tooling, vendor support and extra people.

unified-command-when-there-is-no-single-.core: When an incident spans legitimate jurisdictions (your company and a vendor, two business units, a partner), unified command has each authority's lead jointly set objectives and a single plan, while each keeps control of their own resources.

first_principles.problem: In a cloud-provider-caused outage, your team and the provider's team both act, but with conflicting priorities and no shared plan.
truths: Some incidents have multiple legitimate owners.
No single party can command the others' resources.
derivation: **Agree** joint objectives and one action plan.

analogy.title: A wildfire crossing from forest into a city
analogy.story: Federal and city fire chiefs jointly command, each directing their own crews toward one plan.
analogy.breaks: Unified command needs trust and authority on both sides. Escalate if a party won't engage.

example.title: A payment processor outage
flow: Your IC + processor's incident manager on one bridge
Processor fixes gateway; you enable fallback processor

check.a: When an incident spans several legitimate authorities, such as your company and a vendor, that each control their own resources.

span-of-control-the-pizza-rule.core: One person can effectively supervise about 3–7 people (ideally 5) during an incident. Beyond that, add a layer: section or group leads. This keeps communication manageable, like Amazon's two-pizza team idea.

first_principles.problem: An IC tries to coordinate 25 engineers directly, so messages are lost and nobody is really directed.
derivation: **Contract** the structure as the incident shrinks.

analogy.title: The two-pizza team
analogy.story: If you can't feed the group with two pizzas, it's too big to coordinate directly.
analogy.breaks: Adding layers adds latency, so only expand when needed.

check.q: What should an IC do when more than ~7 people report directly?
check.a: Create sub-groups with their own leads and receive summaries from those leads.
